text: The municipal archive reopened in the spring after a restoration that took the better part of four years. Water had come through the roof of the east wing during a storm and the ledgers stored there were moved into temporary racking while the slates were replaced. Conservators worked through the damaged volumes one at a time, separating the leaves, drying them under weights, and rebinding those that could still be handled. The catalogue that resulted is more detailed than the one it replaced, because every item had to be described again before it was returned to a shelf.

Tidal power has a longer history than most people expect. Mills driven by the rise and fall of an estuary were operating along several European coasts by the twelfth century, grinding grain on a schedule set by the moon rather than by the working day. The modern versions are larger and turn generators instead of millstones, but they inherit the same constraint: the resource is entirely predictable and entirely inflexible. A grid that leans on it has to arrange its other supply around a timetable it cannot negotiate with.

A sourdough culture is a stable community rather than a single organism. Wild yeasts do most of the leavening and lactic acid bacteria do most of the souring, and the two settle into a ratio that depends on how warm the kitchen is and how often the culture is fed. Bakers who move house often report that their starter changes character for a few weeks before settling again. The flour is usually blamed, though the water and the ambient temperature are the more likely causes.

The rail viaduct crosses the valley on twenty-eight arches of local sandstone. It was built by hand between 1846 and 1849 by a workforce that lived in a temporary settlement on the northern slope, and the census taken during construction records masons, labourers, a schoolmaster and two publicans at addresses that no longer exist. The line closed to passengers in 1963 and the structure was left standing because demolition would have cost more than maintenance. It carries a footpath now.

Lichens are not plants and are not really single organisms either. Each one is a partnership between a fungus, which provides the structure and the anchorage, and an alga or a cyanobacterium, which provides the sugars. Because they draw most of what they need from the air rather than from a substrate, they are unusually sensitive to what the air contains, and surveys of which species grow on which walls have been used to map urban pollution since the middle of the nineteenth century.

Bookbinding in the hand-press period was a trade with its own vocabulary and its own hierarchy. A folded sheet was a gathering, the thread that held the gatherings together ran over cords laid across the spine, and the raised bands visible on an old leather binding are those cords showing through the covering. Later binders imitated the bands decoratively long after the structure beneath them had changed, which is why a nineteenth-century book can look older than it is to an untrained eye.

The salt marsh floods twice a day and drains twice a day, and the plants that live there are sorted into bands by how much of that flooding they can tolerate. Glasswort sits lowest and is submerged for hours at a time. Sea lavender and thrift sit higher up and are reached only by the larger tides. Walking out from the sea wall you cross those bands in order, and a botanist can read the height of the ground from the vegetation more quickly than from a level.

Early photographic processes were slow enough that portraits required a sitter to hold still for the better part of a minute. Head rests were built into studio chairs for the purpose, and the resulting expressions are often read as solemnity when they are mostly fatigue. As emulsions improved the exposure fell to a fraction of a second, and the character of the portraits changed with it. The stiffness in the earlier pictures is a property of the chemistry rather than of the century.

A canal lock is a simple machine that trades water for height. Two sets of gates enclose a chamber, sluices let water in from above or out to below, and a boat rises or falls with the level. Every passage sends a chamber's worth of water down the flight, which is why summit levels need reservoirs and why long droughts close canals that look perfectly full. The pumping stations that recycle water back up a flight were among the earliest steam installations in the country.

The double bass is tuned in fourths rather than in fifths like the rest of the string family, a survival from its descent partly from the viol rather than entirely from the violin. This makes the left-hand technique different enough that a cellist cannot simply transfer across. It also explains why orchestral parts written for the instrument sit where they do, and why the lowest string was extended downwards on many modern instruments with a mechanical extension rather than by retuning.

Peat bogs accumulate about a millimetre of material a year in favourable conditions, which means a metre of peat represents roughly a thousand years of growth. Pollen falls onto the surface and is preserved in the waterlogged layers below, so a core taken from a bog reads as a calendar of what was growing nearby. The arrival of cereal pollen and the decline of elm in these records are among the clearest signals of early agriculture available anywhere.

Shipping forecasts are read in a fixed order and a fixed vocabulary because ambiguity at sea is expensive. The sea areas are named and sequenced the same way every time, the wind is given before the weather and the weather before the visibility, and the words used for each are drawn from a closed list. A listener who knows the pattern can extract the part that concerns them without attending to the rest, which is the whole point of the format.

Cast iron and wrought iron behave very differently under load, and confusing the two caused several nineteenth-century structural failures. Cast iron is strong in compression and brittle in tension, so it works well as a column and badly as a beam. Wrought iron tolerates tension and bending. The collapse of a railway bridge in 1847 turned largely on this distinction, and the inquiry that followed did more than any textbook to establish it in the profession.

Vernacular building follows the geology beneath it more closely than any style guide. Where limestone is near the surface the walls are limestone and the roofs are stone slate. Where there is clay the walls are brick and the roofs are tile. Where there is neither, timber framing with an infill of whatever was to hand. The boundaries between these zones on a map of old buildings sit almost exactly on the boundaries between the underlying strata.

Bells are tuned by removing metal from the inside of the bell on a lathe, which lowers particular partials without moving the others by the same amount. A well-tuned bell sounds several partials in a consistent relationship, and the note a listener hears is not necessarily one that is physically present. Founders worked this out empirically over centuries before the acoustics were understood, and a badly tuned recasting can be identified by ear long before it is measured.

The reading room kept its ledgers of admissions from the first year it opened, and the names in them make an unexpectedly good social record. Applicants had to state an occupation and a purpose, and the range of both widens steadily across the century as the rules were relaxed. The earliest volumes are dominated by clergy and lawyers. By the last of them the largest single category is students, and the second largest is people who wrote simply that they wished to read.
